vision_features.abnormalities:

This discoloration is elongated, following the full visible length of the stems from the root-stem junction upward. The affected tissue contrasts sharply with areas of remaining pale cream-to-white healthy-looking pith tissue visible in narrow strips or zones.
2. External stem surface: The outer surface of both stems is dark brown to black, particularly concentrated near the base/root crown area. This darkening is medium to large in extent, covering much of the lower stem exterior. The texture appears dry and somewhat fibrous.
3. Root crown area: At the junction between the stem base and the lateral roots, there is a dense accumulation of dark brown-to-black, dry, fibrous material. This material appears shredded or degraded in texture, approximately 20–30 mm in width across the junction zone.
4. Lateral roots: Several thin, thread-like lateral roots emerge from the crown area. Some appear pale tan-to-white and intact, while others appear dark brown and shriveled or dead. These roots range from very fine (hair-like) to approximately 1–2 mm in diameter.
5. Internal white-to-cream zones: Narrow strips of pale cream or white internal tissue remain visible within the pith of both stems, running longitudinally alongside the darkened tissue. These appear relatively firm and dry compared to the discolored zones.
6. The discoloration pattern in the pith is distributed along the full visible length of both stems, more severe toward the base and somewhat continuous toward the upper portions.
vision_features.absences:

2. No visible raised pustules, tiny raised dots, or thread-like outgrowths on any of the internal cut surfaces.

4. No visible yellowing or pale bleaching of the outer stem surface; the external discoloration is dark brown to black rather than yellow.

The external stem surfaces and root crown area are also heavily darkened and the fibrous tissue at the crown appears degraded and shredded. Narrow strips of pale cream-white tissue remain within the pith, indicating that discoloration is not yet fully uniform across the entire cross-section. The root and lower stem region is the most severely affected area, and the most unusual feature is the dramatic internal browning-to-blackening of the pith running continuously from the base upward in both stems.

Available classes in 'Soybean_Diseases' (3 total):

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Pustule':
────────────────────────────────────────
Bacterial pustule on soybeans presents with lesions found on the outer leaves in the mid- to upper canopy, starting as small, pale green specks with elevated centers. These lesions develop into large, irregularly shaped infected areas. A greenish-yellow halo may surround each lesion, and some lesions may have a pustule in the center, typically located on the lower leaf surface. Unlike bacterial blight, bacterial pustule does not cause leaves to tatter. The disease is favored by hot, wet weather, and it is advisable to avoid planting extremely susceptible soybean varieties where disease is likely. A key difference between bacterial pustule and bacterial blight is that bacterial pustule does not cause leaf tattering, which distinguishes it from the latter.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Fusarium_healthy_vs_infected':
────────────────────────────────────────
Fusarium-infected soybean plants exhibit distinctive symptoms that include brown to reddish-brown lesions primarily on the leaves and stems. These lesions are often sunken, varying in size from 2 to 10 mm, and tend to have irregular shapes with well-defined margins. The infected tissue may show a dry, necrotic appearance with a soft, spongy texture, and can develop a light, powdery coating of mycelium, particularly under humid conditions. Symptoms can also be observed on the roots, which may display a dark discoloration and can show signs of wilting as the disease progresses. In severe cases, the stems may develop gummosis, producing a sticky exudate at the infection site. A key differentiator of Fusarium compared to similar soybean diseases, such as Phytophthora root rot, is the sunken, well-defined lesions with distinct margins on stems and leaves, whereas Phytophthora often presents with more diffuse, spreading, and water-soaked lesions that lack distinct borders.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Phytophthora on soybean manifests as distinctive yellow to brown lesions on the leaves, often with a water-soaked appearance, which can expand and develop dark, irregular edges, creating a prominent contrast against the green foliage. These lesions are frequently sunken and may be accompanied by a characteristic grayish-brown or black mycelial mat on the leaf surface, especially in humid conditions. The stems can exhibit dark, wilting areas that may appear cankerous, while roots show galls or a brown discoloration, leading to reduced plant vigor and stunted growth. Pods may also display dark, sunken spots, contributing to overall poor seed development. The lesions often lack a defined halo but may have a distinct margin that separates healthy tissue from the affected areas. A key visual difference distinguishing Phytophthora from similar diseases like downy mildew is the absence of any powdery, fuzzy growth associated with the latter, which typically appears on the upper leaf surface.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Fusarium_healthy_vs_infected' vs 'Phytophthora'
Ruling feature : Lesion appearance: Fusarium lesions are dry/necrotic with well-defined margins, while Phytophthora lesions are water-soaked and initially yellow with irregular, less distinct borders
Fusarium_healthy_vs_infected: Fusarium produces brown to reddish-brown, sunken, DRY necrotic lesions with well-defined, distinct margins on leaves and stems; a light powdery mycelium coating may appear under humid conditions, and stems may show gummosis (sticky exudate).
Phytophthora: Phytophthora produces yellow to brown lesions with a WATER-SOAKED appearance that expand with dark, irregular edges; a grayish-brown or black mycelial mat may appear on the leaf surface, and lesions lack a defined halo.
Decision rule  : IF lesions appear dry and necrotic with clearly defined, distinct margins and/or a powdery mycelial coating, classify as Fusarium. IF lesions appear water-soaked, yellow-to-brown, with dark irregular expanding edges and a grayish-black mycelial mat (but no powdery coating), classify as Phytophthora.
